title: Commitments
purpose: What this company has promised someone outside it, to whom, by when, and whether it was kept. Read it before promising anything and before telling a client where things stand; record against a commitment rather than opening a second row for the same promise.

fields.name: commitment
fields.description: What was promised, in the words the other side would recognise.

fields.name: to
fields.description: Who it was promised to — the client, user, partner or authority.

fields.name: owner
fields.description: The teammate or desk accountable for delivering it.

fields.name: due
fields.description: When it was promised for. A commitment with no date is a hope.

fields.name: made_on
fields.description: When it was made, which is what settles disagreements about what was said.

fields.name: evidence
fields.description: Where the promise is recorded — the message, the contract clause, the call.

fields.name: progress
fields.description: Where it stands now, in a line, in terms the other side would understand.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: Why it closed — delivered, missed, or released by the other side. Required when it closes.

fields.name: refs
fields.description: Tasks, documents or artifacts that carry the work.

sections.heading: Outstanding
sections.blurb: Promised and not yet delivered. Soonest attention first — record against a row to raise it. If one is not going to land as stated, say so on the row and say what the other side has been told; there is no status that means it, because a status that says how a promise is *going* is one nothing ever moves back out of.

sections.heading: Settled
sections.blurb: Kept, missed, or released — each with the reason. A missed promise is kept here deliberately: it is the company's only honest record of what it costs to say yes, and the thing to read before saying yes the same way again.

writtenBy: `record_entry` to make or update a promise, `close_entry` when it is kept, missed or released

title: Learnings
purpose: What this company has found out — from a run, a launch, a client, a failure — and what it should change. Read it before repeating something the company has already tried; record one whenever a result surprised you, including when it went well.

fields.name: learning
fields.description: What is now known, stated so somebody could act on it without reading the rest.

fields.name: evidence
fields.description: What actually happened, concretely. A learning with no evidence is an opinion with a row of its own.

fields.name: so_what
fields.description: What should be done differently next time. The half that makes this worth writing.

fields.name: owner
fields.description: The teammate or desk that found it, and can be asked about it.

fields.name: confidence
fields.description: How sure — one run, a pattern across many, or a client saying it outright.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: Why it closed — adopted into a standard, or shown wrong. Required when it closes.

fields.name: refs
fields.description: The run, task, decision or document it came out of.

sections.heading: Confirmed
sections.blurb: Seen more than once, or stated plainly by someone outside. Treat these as true until something says otherwise.

sections.heading: Noted
sections.blurb: Seen once. Worth knowing, not yet worth building on.

sections.heading: Closed
sections.blurb: Adopted into how the company works, or disproved — each with the reason. A disproved learning is kept precisely because it is the one somebody would otherwise re-derive from the same single run.

writtenBy: `record_entry` to add or revise a learning, `close_entry` when it is folded into practice or superseded

title: Risks
purpose: What could stop this company doing what it said it would, who is watching each one, and what would be done if it happened. Read it before committing to a date or a deal; record against a risk when its likelihood changes rather than opening a new row.

fields.name: risk
fields.description: What could go wrong, stated as the thing that happens rather than the worry about it.

fields.name: owner
fields.description: The teammate or desk watching it. A risk nobody owns is a risk nobody notices moving.

fields.name: impact
fields.description: What it costs if it happens — money, a date, a client, a licence.

fields.name: likelihood
fields.description: How likely, in a word or two, and why that answer rather than a lower one.

fields.name: trigger
fields.description: The observable that says this is happening now, so watching it is a check and not a feeling.

fields.name: response
fields.description: What would actually be done. A risk with no response is a note.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: Why it closed — retired, realised, or accepted as a cost. Required when it closes.

fields.name: refs
fields.description: Tasks, decisions or documents that carry the work of mitigating it.

sections.heading: Happening now
sections.blurb: Realised, and being dealt with. Anything here outranks anything below it.

sections.heading: Being mitigated
sections.blurb: Someone is actively reducing these. Record against a row to raise it.

sections.heading: Watched
sections.blurb: Named, owned, and not being worked — each with the trigger that would change that.

sections.heading: Settled
sections.blurb: No longer tracked, or materialised and dealt with — each with the reason, which is where retired (it is gone) and accepted (we are living with it) are told apart. Kept: a risk accepted without a recorded reason is one somebody re-raises next month, and a realised one is the company's only record of what it actually cost.

writtenBy: `record_entry` to raise or re-assess a risk, `close_entry` when it is retired, realised or accepted

title: Incidents
purpose: Everything that has gone wrong in production: what broke, who is on it, what customers were told, and what was changed so it does not happen again. Read it before shipping near a system that has broken before; open a row the moment something is wrong, not once it is understood.

fields.name: incident
fields.description: What is broken, from the customer's side rather than the stack's.

fields.name: severity
fields.description: sev1 (customers cannot work), sev2 (degraded), sev3 (contained). Guess high; downgrading is cheap.

fields.name: owner
fields.description: The one teammate driving it. Not a desk — an incident with two owners has none.

fields.name: started_at
fields.description: When it began, as opposed to when it was noticed. The gap is itself a finding.

fields.name: impact
fields.description: Who was affected and how, in numbers if there are any.

fields.name: told_customers
fields.description: What was said publicly and when. Blank here after a sev1 is its own problem.

fields.name: cause
fields.description: What actually caused it, once known. `unknown` is an honest value; a plausible guess written as fact is not.

fields.name: prevention
fields.description: The change that stops a repeat, and the task id carrying it. A resolved incident with no prevention is a rehearsal.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: How it ended. Required when it closes.

fields.name: refs
fields.description: Tasks, commits, dashboards and the customer thread.

sections.heading: Open now
sections.blurb: Live. Nothing else this roster is doing outranks a row here.

sections.heading: Mitigated, not resolved
sections.blurb: Customers are working again and the cause is still there. These are the ones that come back — each should name the task that finishes it.

sections.heading: Closed
sections.blurb: Resolved, with the cause and the prevention. Kept: the fastest way to diagnose an outage is to find the last one that looked like it.

writtenBy: `record_entry` to open or update an incident, `close_entry` when it is resolved and the follow-up is filed

title: Releases
purpose: Every version put in front of customers: what went out, when, who approved it, and what had to be rolled back. Read it before diagnosing anything that started recently, and before telling a customer what they are running.

fields.name: id
fields.description: The version, as customers would see it — `2026.08.3`, not `sprint-14`.

fields.name: release
fields.description: What this release is, in one line a customer would understand.

fields.name: owner
fields.description: Who cut it and is watching it.

fields.name: contents
fields.description: What changed, grouped as customers experience it rather than as commits.

fields.name: risk
fields.description: What could go wrong with this specific release, and what is being watched to catch it.

fields.name: rollback
fields.description: How to undo it, written before it goes out. A release with no rollback plan is not ready.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: Why it closed — fully rolled out, or pulled and why. Required when it closes.

fields.name: refs
fields.description: Tasks, tags, and the incident row if one followed.

sections.heading: In flight
sections.blurb: Staged or rolling out. Watch these before starting anything new.

sections.heading: Shipped
sections.blurb: Out, or pulled — each with the reason. This is the timeline an incident is correlated against, so the dates matter more than the prose.

writtenBy: `record_entry` to cut or update a release, `close_entry` when it is fully rolled out or rolled back

title: Security findings
purpose: Vulnerabilities and weaknesses known to this company: where, how bad, whether anyone outside knows, and what has been shipped about it. Read it before touching auth, payments, uploads or anything customer-isolating.

fields.name: finding
fields.description: What an attacker could do, stated as the outcome and not the code smell.

fields.name: severity
fields.description: critical / high / medium / low, judged on what it lets somebody do — not on how hard it was to find.

fields.name: surface
fields.description: The endpoint, dependency or flow it lives in.

fields.name: reported_by
fields.description: Internal review, a scanner, or somebody outside — which decides whether there is a clock.

fields.name: exploitability
fields.description: What an attacker needs first. A finding requiring database access already is not the same as one requiring a URL.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: How it closed — the fix, the mitigation, or why it is not exploitable. Required when it closes.

fields.name: refs
fields.description: The task, the patch, the advisory, the release it went out in.

sections.heading: Confirmed and unfixed
sections.blurb: Real, reproducible, and still there. Anything critical here outranks feature work.

sections.heading: Triaging
sections.blurb: Reported, not yet confirmed. Say what would settle it.

sections.heading: Closed
sections.blurb: Fixed, mitigated, or judged not exploitable — each with the reason and the release it went out in. A `not_exploitable` row with no reasoning is the one that gets re-reported by the next scanner and re-dismissed from memory.

writtenBy: `record_entry` to raise or re-assess a finding, `close_entry` when it is fixed, mitigated or judged not exploitable
